title: Patient Recall for Specialty Practices: How to Bring Back the 46% Who Miss Their Follow-Up
summary: Only 54% of follow-up patients return on schedule. See what late and lost patients are worth per physician and how voice AI brings them back.
body_markdown:
Patient recall (also called patient re-engagement or reactivation) is outreach that brings existing patients back for follow-up care they're due for. Only 54% of follow-up patients return on schedule. Prosper AI's[2026 Growth Report](https://www.getprosper.ai/report/specialty-revenue-growth-2026) estimates that recalling late and lost patients is worth $37,400 per physician each year.


Every specialty practice has patients who were told to come back in 6 months and didn't. Your team won't notice, because an unbooked follow-up never shows up as a hole in the schedule.


Prosper AI's[2026 Growth Report](https://www.getprosper.ai/report/specialty-revenue-growth-2026) sizes that drift at an estimated $37,400 per physician per year, the second-biggest of the 4 revenue levers. For a 20-physician practice, that's nearly $750,000 a year in patients who are already in your EHR.


**TL;DR**


- Only 54% of patients due for a follow-up return on schedule. 40% come back late, and 6% never return.
- Bringing late and lost patients back is worth an estimated $37,400 per physician per year, rising to $63,000 in dermatology.
- No-shows average 18.8% across medical specialties, and 32% of medical groups saw more of them in 2026.
- Reminder texts confirm visits that are already booked. Recall lists wait for a quiet front desk.
- An AI voice agent calls overdue patients, books into your EHR and confirms what the visit will cost before the patient comes in.


## How many follow-up patients actually come back?


Only 54% of specialty patients due for a follow-up visit come back on schedule. Another 40% return late, and 6% never return at all, according to Prosper AI's[2026 Growth Report](https://www.getprosper.ai/report/specialty-revenue-growth-2026) .


Here's what that looks like for every 100 patients due for a follow-up:


Outcome Patients out of 100 What outreach changes


Return on schedule 54 Already back on time


Come back late 40 Outreach brings them back closer to the due date: 15% more visits


Never return 6 Outreach wins back 10% of them


Most of the opportunity sits with the 40% who come back late. They still return, but every month past the due date is a visit that doesn't happen that year. Think of the annual skin check that slips to month 16, or the 6-month post-op visit that turns into 9.


None of it shows up in a report. A no-show leaves a visible hole in tomorrow's schedule. A patient who never books a follow-up leaves nothing behind, so no one tracks the visit that didn't happen.


## How common are no-shows in specialty practices?


[No-shows average 18.8%](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4714455/) across medical specialties, and gastroenterology runs highest at 25.7%.[Dermatology no-show rates](https://www.jaad.org/article/S0190-9622(24)00978-2/fulltext) range from 12% to 31% depending on clinic type.


Missed visits often stay missed. A[Massachusetts General Hospital dermatology study](https://mdedge.com/content/factors-associated-missed-dermatology-appointments) found that nearly 19% of appointments were missed, and only 41% of those patients returned to the practice within the following year.


The trend is getting worse. In an[August 2026 MGMA Stat poll](https://www.mgma.com/mgma-stat/about-1-in-3-medical-groups-see-higher-no-shows-in-2026-as-patients-face-higher-costs) , 32% of medical groups reported more no-shows than in 2025, while 10% reported fewer.


For tactics on the day-of side, see our[guide to reducing no-shows](https://www.getprosper.ai/blog/reduce-no-shows-healthcare-guide) . The rest of this post covers the bigger gap: patients who never get back on the schedule.


## How much revenue can specialty practices recover from late and lost patients?


Bringing late and lost patients back is worth an estimated $37,400 a year for the average specialty physician, according to Prosper AI's[2026 Growth Report](https://www.getprosper.ai/report/specialty-revenue-growth-2026) . That's a 6.6% lift on the $568K in recurring revenue a physician brings in:

If you run patient access, this is the cheapest growth on the table. You already paid to acquire these patients, and they're already in your EHR. The only missing piece is the call that books them.


The number moves a lot by specialty. Here's the estimated re-engagement opportunity per full-time physician, from the same model run against each specialty's MGMA benchmarks:

Now multiply by headcount. A 20-physician dermatology group is looking at about **$1.26M a year in re-engagement opportunity alone** , before you count[missed calls](https://www.getprosper.ai/blog/missed-calls-specialty-practices) , denials or unpaid balances.


## Why don't reminder texts and manual recall lists bring patients back?


Reminder texts only work on visits that are already booked, and recall lists only get worked when someone has time to dial. Neither one books the patient who drifted off the schedule.


A one-way text can't answer "can I come Thursday instead?" or "what will this cost me?" So the patient has to call the front desk to sort it out, and that's where the follow-up stalls. We compare reminder channels in more depth in[AI calls vs. SMS and email reminders](https://www.getprosper.ai/blog/ai-appointment-reminders-voice-vs-sms-email) .


Manual recall has the opposite problem. A person on the phone can answer every question, but only when they're free to dial out. At the average specialty practice, the front desk already[misses 18% of inbound calls](https://www.getprosper.ai/blog/missed-calls-specialty-practices) during office hours. Outbound recall waits behind all of it.


So the list grows. Every week it sits, more of the 40% drift further past their due date, and a few more join the 6% who never come back.

The row that decides it is the fourth one. A patient who's worried about the bill doesn't rebook from a text, and that worry is growing.


## What should specialty groups look for in patient recall software?


The best patient recall software for a multi-location specialty group pulls overdue patients from your EHR, calls them, books the visit and confirms what it will cost. Check these 6 things before you shortlist:


1. **Recall lists from your EHR.** It should find due and overdue patients by your recall rules, at every location, without staff exporting a spreadsheet.
2. **Two-way conversations.** The patient should be able to ask for a different day, or a different location, and get booked on the same call.
3. **EHR write-back.** The booking, a call summary and any updated insurance details should land in the chart.
4. **Cost answers on the call.** Ask whether it can check eligibility and benefits and tell the patient what they'll owe. That's the question that keeps people from rebooking.
5. **Rules per specialty and site.** An annual skin check, a surveillance colonoscopy and a post-op visit follow different timing. The agent should know the difference.
6. **Security paperwork.** A signed BAA and a current SOC 2 Type II report.


## Does cost fear keep patients from coming back?


Often, yes. The Growth Report links rising no-shows to cost pressure on patients, and the same[MGMA poll](https://www.mgma.com/mgma-stat/about-1-in-3-medical-groups-see-higher-no-shows-in-2026-as-patients-face-higher-costs) that found more no-shows in 2026 tied them to higher patient costs. Patients now pay 36% of the cost of their care on average across specialty practices, and 55% in dermatology.


So the fix starts before the visit. A patient who knows their coverage and what they'll owe has one less reason to skip.


That's why Prosper AI books[benefit-verified appointments](https://www.getprosper.ai/blog/benefits-verification-guide-healthcare-providers) : coverage confirmed and the patient's cost explained before the visit. The same agent that books the follow-up also[checks eligibility](https://www.getprosper.ai/blog/insurance-eligibility-verification-complete-guide) and flags visits that need[prior authorization](https://www.getprosper.ai/blog/prior-authorization-automation-guide) . When that takes a payer call, it makes the call.


Getting the front end right pays off twice more after the visit. Front-end errors drive about 45% of first-submission denials, worth an estimated $28,500 per physician a year. And a patient who heard their balance up front is easier to collect from, worth $14,100 per physician.


A recalled patient only counts if they show up and the claim gets paid.


## How do you run patient recall across multiple locations?


Run recall from your EHR, on the same rules at every location: find patients who are due or overdue, reach them, book the visit and write it back to the chart. Here's how to set it up in 5 steps:


1. **Pull the list from your EHR.** Report on patients past their follow-up date or recall interval, built per location with that site's recall rules. A list that refreshes from the EHR beats a spreadsheet someone exports once a quarter.
2. **Reach patients by phone first.** A call lets the patient ask about timing and cost and book on the spot, at the location they want. Use texts to follow up with patients who don't pick up.
3. **Write it back and route the rest.** Every booking and a short call summary should land back in the chart, so staff never re-key a note later. Clinical questions go to your staff.
4. **Start with one recall cohort.** Pick a follow-up type with clear timing rules, such as annual skin checks in dermatology or surveillance colonoscopies in GI. Prove the lift there, then add cohorts and locations.
5. **Track it weekly.** Watch 3 numbers: overdue patients reached, follow-ups booked per 100 patients called and the show rate on recalled visits.


## Frequently asked questions


**What's a good no-show rate for a specialty practice?**


The average no-show rate across medical specialties is 18.8% and gastroenterology runs highest at 25.7%, according to a 2026 study in BMC Health Services Research. Beating your specialty's average is a good start. Also track how many missed visits get rebooked: MGMA found only 27.4% of canceled visits are rescheduled within 30 days.


**How do dermatology practices reduce no-shows?**


Dermatology no-show rates range from 12% to 31% depending on clinic type, according to a JAAD study, and patients pay 55% of the cost of their dermatology care. The fixes that work target both: confirm coverage and cost before the visit, and call patients due for annual skin checks. Prosper AI's 2026 Growth Report sizes dermatology re-engagement at $63K per physician a year.


**How do I get overdue patients back on the schedule?**


Pull every patient past their follow-up date from your EHR, then call them with the option to book on the same call. Prosper AI's 2026 Growth Report estimates that outreach brings late patients back closer to their due date, adding 15% more visits, and wins back 10% of patients who would otherwise never return.


**Does AI recall work for patients who don't answer texts?**


Yes. A voice agent calls the patient directly, so it reaches people who ignore texts or never log in to the portal. When a patient calls back, Prosper AI answers 24/7 and can book the visit on that call.


**Can it reschedule a no-show automatically?**


Yes. Prosper AI can call a patient after a missed appointment, offer open slots and write the new booking into your EHR, so the visit gets rebooked without staff working a list.


**Can it answer "what will this cost me?" on the call?**


Yes. The agent can check the patient's eligibility and benefits and explain their expected cost before booking. When the answer needs a payer, Prosper AI calls the payer, so the follow-up arrives benefit-verified.


**Is automated patient outreach HIPAA compliant?**


It can be, and you should[ask every vendor for proof](https://www.getprosper.ai/blog/patient-outreach-hipaa-compliant-ai-strategies) . Prosper AI is HIPAA-compliant, SOC 2 Type II certified, and signs a BAA with every customer.
